confirmed: Read the complete markdown conversion and checked all 12 PDF pages, including the appendix. The title, three authors, CEUR Workshop Proceedings identification, and HAIC 2025 event dated October 25, 2025 match the form; the Vol-4072/paper1 identifier comes from the retrieval source URL (PDF p. 1; retrieval.json c706.source_url).

The reported cohort consists of 13 male students from the University of Bologna Intelligent Robotic Systems course, with 7 using LLM assistance and 6 without; these are people, not code pairs or simulation runs. No exclusions or separate participant-flow counts are reported, and no randomized headcount is given; the sample is below 50 regardless (PDF p. 3, Section 3; pp. 5-6, results).

The paper contains one assistance comparison, not an AI-only versus human-only benchmark or a synthesis. The reported DAT-balanced allocation supports retaining the comparison as quasi_people/observational context rather than identifying a documented RCT; core=no and the fewer-than-50 decision remain appropriate (PDF pp. 3-5, Sections 3-4).

Microsoft Copilot was used through its online interface in its May 2025 version, in required incognito mode; Quick Response and Think Deeper were available, and students in the assistance group had to query it at least three times (PDF p. 4, Section 3; p. 9, reference 26).

The task was a Lua path-following controller for a simulated Foot-Bot in ARGoS3, during an experiment lasting three hours; the evaluation function was shown to the students (PDF pp. 3-4, Section 3 and Equation 1).

There were three development arenas and two test arenas. The evaluation used 100 runs per controller per arena, with a limit of 5 minutes of simulation; Figure 3 labels the noise conditions 1x and 5x. These repetitions are not additional people (PDF p. 4, Figure 2; p. 5, Figure 3 and Section 4).

Dolos similarity is computed on pairs of controllers produced by different students within an assistance group, so it is an output-scored across_people diversity measure with unit=pair. The reported qualitative result is higher similarity with Copilot, but no exact median, effect size, p-value, or confidence interval is printed (PDF p. 5, Section 4; p. 6, Figure 4).

The performance reported string reproduces the results narrative: the no-LLM group did better on average, Copilot produced the highest performances on development arenas, and Copilot performance dropped under higher noise while the other group was described as overall stable. The same performance direction in the one-line finding is supported; these remain qualitative statements without numerical effect estimates (PDF p. 5, Figure 3 and Section 4).

The internal appendix contains DAT distributions and NCD alternatives in Figures 6-7, self-reported coding experience and time in Figures 8-9, and qualitative student comments in Table 1. DAT is a pre-task grouping measure and the experience/time reports are not creativity scores on produced output; no separate supplement or additional experiment is cited (PDF pp. 10-12, Appendix; p. 4, DAT procedure).
This is an original small experiment, not a review or meta-analysis; the empty synthesis estimates and null synthesis counts are appropriate (PDF pp. 3-7, Sections 3-6).
summary: The full workshop paper reports one DAT-balanced comparison of 13 students (7 with Copilot, 6 without), with randomization unreported; core exclusion and observational context remain appropriate. Corrections remove graph-estimated medians, qualify assignment claims, fix the internet-access description, and complete contrast and diversity-method fields.
